analytic.title: Designing Usable User Interfaces of Digital Twins: Benefits and Limitations of Applying the User Centered Design Process

meeting.title: HCSE 2026 - 11th International Working Conference on Human-Centered Software Engineering

abstract.p: The User Centered Design (UCD) process is dedicated to the design and development of systems and software focusing on their usability. Identified in the mid eighties, this process revolves around the notions of users tasks and work context, design solutions identification and evaluation of those solutions with representative users. This process is, by nature, iterative, as the goal of the evaluation is to identify areas of improvements in the solutions proposed, leading to refined and improved solutions. This process was identified in the context of computerization of human activities, i.e. transforming work with the support of computerbased automation. Digital Twins (DTs) connected to a Cyber-Physical System (CPS) (also called Physical Twin (PT)), could fall under such a computerization approach, but with specificities including: the potential critical nature of the PT; the complexity of the tasks of the operators of the PT; or the unknown tasks that new users of the DT would have to perform on it. This paper identifies challenges brought by the design, development and evaluation of User Interfaces (UIs) of DTs due to these specificities. It describes the limitations of the UCD process and presents a set of extensions to address the specific issues brought by the design and evaluation of UIs of DTs. These extensions are made concrete on the real-world case study of a DT of the electric grid in Luxembourg.

imprint.biblScope: IHM’26 : Actes étendus de la 37ème conférence Francophone sur l’Interaction Humain-Machine

abstract.p: There are several types of developer. First, those whose profes- sion is related to software development, such as software engineers, business experts and testers. Then, professionals whose work re- quires development without it being the main objective, such as sci- entists. Finally, there are citizens, including non-programmers, who sometimes want to understand or manipulate software artefacts, in order to solve their own problems or verify a public administra- tion’s application. Despite their different development activities and needs, all these developers must deal with the growing com- plexity of software artefacts. This is why DevX is emerging as a research field aimed at improving the developer experience in terms of creativity, engagement, accessibility, confidence, social translu- cency, and the balance between satisfaction and efficiency when interacting with software artefacts. The field of human-computer interaction (HCI) generally studies these aspects of DevX through the lens of software usability and user experience. This positioning article aims to identify areas of collaboration between HCI and DevX fields for studying developer experience. To this end, we transpose HCI concepts to a DevX framework, expose the limits of this transposition, and map developer profiles to the HCI sub-fields relevant to their activities.

Il existe plusieurs profils de développeurs. Celles et ceux dont la profession est liée au développement logiciel, comme les ingénieurs logiciels, les experts métiers ou encore les testeurs. Mais aussi les professionnels dont le métier nécessite de développer sans que ce soit leur objectif principal, comme les scientifiques. Et enfin, les ci- toyens en général, même non-programmeurs, qui souhaitent parfois comprendre ou manipuler des artefacts logiciels, par exemple pour résoudre leurs propres problèmes, ou vérifier une application insti- tutionnelle. Malgré des activités de développement et des besoins différents, ces profils doivent tous faire face à la complexité crois- sante des artefacts logiciels. C’est pourquoi le DevX émerge comme champ de recherche visant à améliorer l’expérience développeur, c’est-à-dire la créativité, l’engagement, l’accessibilité, la confiance, la translucence sociale, ainsi que l’équilibre entre satisfaction et ef- ficacité lors des interactions avec des artefacts logiciels. Ces aspects du DevX sont généralement étudiés par le domaine des interactions humain-machine (IHM) au travers de l’axe de l’utilisabilité logi- cielle et de l’expérience utilisateur. Cet article de positionnement vise à identifier les travaux communs qui peuvent être menés entre les domaine scientifique de l’IHM et du DevX. Dans cet objectif, nous transposons les notions de l’IHM en les instanciant dans un cadre DevX, montrons les limites de cette transposition, et formu- lons une correspondance entre les profils de développeurs et les sous-disciplines de l’IHM pertinentes pour leurs activités.

analytic.title: LivEx: Enabling Live Programming over a Distributed Execution State

monogr.title: The Art, Science, and Engineering of Programming

abstract.p:
Program comprehension is challenging when the execution state is distributed across heterogeneous platforms (e.g., CPUs, virtual machines...) or multiple languages with isolated runtimes. Developers are typically restricted to local execution views, which hinders the understanding and reasoning about global program behavior.

Existing tools such as debuggers, loggers, and live programming environments expose only local states of a single programming language. This prevents understanding how local changes affect the global state involving multiple languages. It raises two key challenges: (i) accessing a coherent global state from distributed local states, and (ii) enabling developers to reason about it effectively from their own local context.

In this paper, we extend example-based live programming to address these challenges. We introduce LivEx, a domain specific language that allows developers to specify, directly at a given place of interest in the program, not only examples but also the corresponding execution entry points and probes which allow querying information on the global state. This mechanism centralizes distributed states into a unified live view, accessible from the developer's local context.

Our implementation demonstrates that LivEx allows the construction of a coherent global view from distributed local states and supports tracking the propagation of changes across platforms and languages. We evaluate our approach by examining 1) its applicability, which we find to require a low-to-moderate amount of effort; 2) its responsiveness, which scales linearly with the number of probe elements; and 3) its expressiveness, which we find to cover various use-cases.

LivEx enables developers to access and visualize, from their local context, the impact of their work on the overall global execution state.

analytic.title: Spec2COBOLRot: An Agentic-AI Degradation Loop for Realistic COBOL Corpus Generation

meeting.title: AISM 2026 - 2nd International Workshop on AI for Software Modernization co-located with Automated Software Engineering Conference

keywords.term: Software and its engineering → Software maintenance tools Automated Software Engineering COBOL Generation Large Languages Models

abstract.p: COBOL remains widely deployed, yet representative corpora reflecting real production code are rarely available, limiting rigorous benchmarking of modernization approaches. We propose a systematic agentic AI pipeline for generating realistic COBOL programs, combining specification-driven generation with iterative degradation guided by patterns and complexity targets extracted from real production code. Here, realism is understood as structural fidelity to production code as captured by our metrics. We evaluate whether degradation reaches target complexity levels while preserving business behavior, and examine the limits of the approach, across three programs from distinct business domains. Results show the pipeline reliably produces syntactically valid programs and moves them toward realistic structural complexity. However, preserving business behavior is not always achieved by construction, and targeting structural metrics independently of business logic risks producing programs whose complexity does not reflect a plausible maintenance history. We discuss these limitations and outline a more realistic alternative as a direction for future work, generating legacy programs from scratch along a simulated development history.

analytic.title: System Test Generation for Virtual Reality Applications using Scenario Models

abstract.p: Virtual Reality (VR) applications are increasingly being integrated across a wide range of domains, including surgical training and industrial marketing. However, the long-term adoption and maintenance of VR applications remain limited, particularly due to the lack of effective, systematic, and reproducible software testing approaches tailored to their unique characteristics. To address this issue, we introduce UltraInstinctVR, a novel testing approach for VR applications. Relying on predefined VR models (scenarios), it automates the generation and execution of concrete VR system tests. In our empirical evaluation, we compare UltraInstinctVR with state-of-the-art automated VR testing approaches in terms of coverage and failure detection on 10 open-source VR applications. The results show that UltraInstinctVR outperforms existing automated tools for detecting unique failures and provides valuable insights for identifying real-world bugs in VR applications.

monogr.title: Proceedings of the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE ’26)

abstract.p: Virtual Reality (VR) applications are increasingly used in domains such as surgical training and industrial marketing, yet their longterm adoption remains limited by the lack of effective, systematic, and reproducible testing approaches tailored to VR. To address this gap, we present UltraInstinctVR, a novel tool that automates the generation and execution of concrete system-level tests for VR applications, helping developers efficiently validate interactions and behaviors. We evaluated UltraInstinctVR against state-of-the-art automated VR testing tools across 10 open-source VR applications, where it outperformed existing approaches in detecting unique failures and uncovering real-world bugs. In this paper, we further extended this evaluation through an empirical user study with ten VR developers. Results highlight strong dependability and efficiency while identifying opportunities for improvement in other user experience dimensions. Overall, these findings position UltraInstinct-VR as a promising step toward more practical, effective, and scalable VR testing. The tool is publicly available at https://github.com/snail- unamur/UltraInstinctVR, with a demonstration video available at https://youtu.be/U8DWTmXmeh4.
